Circular.Awareness: Map all organic waste and nutrient-rich effluent streams from operations to identify the highest-potential sources for valorization and the associated emission reduction from avoiding landfill methane and reducing virgin resource use.
Circular.Developing: Develop and launch certified low-carbon fertilizer products that clearly communicate their reduced GHG footprint due to circular sourcing, targeting customers and markets with climate commitments.
Circular.Leading: Champion the integration of circular nutrient management into national climate strategies (NDCs) by sharing data, participating in policy dialogues, and advocating for incentives that reward carbon-smart fertilizer production.

Environmental.Awareness: Provide operations, logistics and maintenance teams with an introductory workshop on the relevance of energy consumption, transport fuel use, and emissions reduction in the fertilizer supply chain. Encourage staff to propose 2–3 “quick wins”
Environmental.Developing: Use your baseline to set SMART goals (e.g., X% reduction in energy per tonne product, Y% of transport fuel from renewable sources, Z% reduction in CO₂eq by year Y). Embed into budgeting and capital planning to ensure projects are recognised.
Environmental.Leading: Incorporate emissions and climate resilience metrics (e.g., carbon‑intensity per tonne product, % renewable energy share, reduction in transport emissions) into annual sustainability reports, aligned with frameworks (e.g., ISO 14064, GRI, CDP). Use this to enhance investor & stakeholder confidence and internal accountability.

Economic.Awareness: Conduct a climate risk and opportunity assessment using the TCFD framework to identify transition risks (e.g., carbon pricing, shifts in demand) and physical risks (e.g., drought, flooding) that could impact financial performance.
Economic.Developing: Allocate a defined percentage of the R&D budget to the development of low-carbon and climate-resilient products, such as enhanced-efficiency fertilizers or green ammonia, linking product development to climate strategy.
Economic.Leading: Integrate climate performance metrics (e.g., revenue from low-carbon products, progress on decarbonization) into executive compensation schemes and long-term corporate strategy, making climate accountability a board-level priority.

Social.Awareness: Provide short, bite‑sized content (e‑mail links, posters, videos) covering climate change risks and relevance to production, procurement and operations. Use multilingual formats if your workforce is diverse.
Social.Developing: For each function (e.g., production, logistics, sales, maintenance) design short training (2‑3 hours) on how climate change impacts the value chain (e.g., raw‑material scarcity, extreme weather, supply chain disruption) and what mitigation/adaptation actions staff in that role can take.
Social.Leading: Make climate‑adaptation/mitigation training part of the company’s standard induction, annual refresher programmes and manager competency requirements. Link participation and knowledge uptake to performance reviews and leadership development.

Circular.Awareness: Deliver introductory sessions for employees on how nutrient runoff affects marine ecosystems (eutrophication, dead zones) and how circular practices like nutrient recovery, recycling, and reuse can mitigate these impacts.
Circular.Developing: Introduce redesigned production and packaging processes to reduce plastic and chemical leakage (e.g., returnable packaging, waste-to-resource loops). Ensure alignment with marine biodiversity protection objectives.
Circular.Leading: Embed nutrient recovery, by-product valorization, and zero-leakage systems into long-term corporate planning. Monitor impacts specifically on marine ecosystems and publicly report reductions.

Environmental.Awareness: Benchmark current effluent quality against the EU's Water Framework Directive and other stringent regional standards to assess compliance risks and identify gaps in pollution control.
Environmental.Developing: Implement a robust water quality monitoring and management system with real-time sensors and regular laboratory testing to ensure continuous compliance with internal and external effluent standards
Environmental.Leading: Champion a "Zero Harmful Discharge" ambition by investing in circular nutrient recovery systems that treat wastewater as a resource, extracting nutrients for reuse in fertilizers and closing the loop to prevent marine pollution entirely.

Economic.Awareness: Conduct a basic internal assessment mapping how fertilizer nutrient losses contribute to marine pollution (eutrophication hotspots) and the potential economic benefits of innovations like slow-release or stabilized fertilizers.
Economic.Developing: Collaborate with research organizations to co-develop or test nutrient-efficient fertilizers that reduce marine eutrophication while ensuring product performance, affordability, and market acceptance.
Economic.Leading: Dedicate a portion of annual investment to scaling low-leaching formulations, recovering nutrients from waste streams, and redesigning products to outperform competitors in sustainability and cost efficiency.

Social.Awareness: Partner with a marine research institution to conduct a literature review and develop an internal briefing on the links between fertilizer-derived nitrogen runoff, coastal eutrophication, and ocean acidification.
Social.Developing: Co-fund and participate in a local or regional scientific monitoring program with research bodies to track nutrient levels in watersheds that lead to sensitive coastal areas.
Social.Leading: Establish and fund an "Ocean Health and Sustainable Agriculture" innovation prize or grant program for scientists and NGOs to develop new solutions for preventing nutrient runoff, positioning the company as a leader in the field.

Circular.Awareness: Offer introductory staff training on how sourcing organic waste reduces land degradation, desertification, and virgin resource dependency.
Circular.Developing: SMEs collaborate with local agricultural producers or biogas operators to begin sourcing manure, compost, and digestate to substitute part of the virgin raw materials.
Circular.Leading: SMEs fully embed nutrient-loop sourcing (organic waste, manure, digestate) into procurement policies and long-term supply contracts, reducing dependence on virgin materials and decreasing land degradation impacts.

Environmental.Awareness: Conduct a comprehensive pre-mining baseline assessment of soil health, biodiversity, and hydrology at extraction sites to establish a scientific benchmark for post-mining restoration goals.
Environmental.Developing: Develop and implement a Mine Closure and Rehabilitation Plan that is integrated into the mining lifecycle from the outset, with dedicated financial provisioning (e.g., a rehabilitation bond or fund).
Environmental.Leading: Publicly disclose key performance indicators on rehabilitation, such as the percentage of disturbed land under active restoration and the hectares of land successfully rehabilitated to a pre-agreed productive or ecological state.

Economic.Awareness: Conduct a baseline review of financial allocations (R&D, operations, sourcing) to determine where biodiversity, soil restoration, or sustainable land-use investments are currently lacking.
Economic.Developing: Assign small but targeted funds to pilot projects such as soil-rebuilding initiatives, landscape restoration, or biodiversity-friendly farming practices with upstream suppliers.
Economic.Leading: Commit substantial financial resources to large-scale regenerative programs (e.g., cover cropping, erosion control, soil carbon enhancement) through partnerships with farmers and communities.

Social.Awareness: Develop and deliver mandatory foundational training for all R&D, production, and agronomic staff on the principles of soil health and the links between fertilizer use and ecosystem impacts (e.g., eutrophication, soil biodiversity loss).
Social.Developing: Create and disseminate detailed "Ecosystem Protection Guidelines" for internal production (to prevent pollution) and for sales agronomists (to advise farmers on application practices that minimize runoff and protect nearby wetlands and forests).
Social.Leading: Establish a certification or bonus incentive program for employees who demonstrate exceptional leadership in integrating ecosystem protection into their work, and partner with universities to develop a certified curriculum for "Sustainable Fertilizer Management."

Circular.Awareness: Begin by identifying all recycled inputs (e.g., compost, digestate, industrial by-products) and reviewing whether labeling, SDS, and communication meet minimum standards.
Circular.Developing: Implement improved labeling that clearly states recycled material content, origin (e.g., manure, digestate, biomass ash), and safety handling details, supported by publicly available SDS.
Circular.Leading: Offer customers real-time access to recovery method details, recycled-input percentages, and environmental profiles of fertilizer products.

Environmental.Awareness: Conduct a materiality assessment in accordance with GRI Standards to identify the most significant environmental, social, and governance (ESG) risks and impacts of your fertilizer production to determine what to disclose
Environmental.Developing: Publish an annual sustainability report aligned with GRI Standards that discloses the results of your risk assessments, and actively share this report with key stakeholders, including local communities, suppliers, and investors.
Environmental.Leading: Establish a multi-stakeholder advisory panel, including community representatives, NGOs, and academics, to review sustainability performance, validate assessment methodologies, and provide input on the company's long-term environmental strategy.

Economic.Awareness: Create a short, clear policy that defines acceptable and unacceptable practices related to supplier selection, purchasing, incentives, and subsidy use.
Economic.Developing: Use due diligence checklists, conflict-of-interest declarations, and supplier background checks to ensure fairness in sourcing.
Economic.Leading: Adopt digital procurement systems that track bids, pricing, and subsidy allocation, providing auditable trails and reducing human discretion.

Social.Awareness: Conduct confidential surveys and focus groups with employees, suppliers, and smallholder farmers to identify key sustainability concerns and gauge interest in participation mechanisms.
Social.Developing: Establish a formal "Sustainability Committee" or "Green Team" with rotating, elected representatives from different employee levels and departments to provide input on environmental policies and goals.
Social.Leading: Appoint a designated "Stakeholder Ombudsperson" and implement a transparent grievance mechanism that allows employees and value chain partners to raise sustainability concerns anonymously and without fear of reprisal.

Circular.Awareness: Identify EU, national, and regional funding programs (e.g., Horizon Europe, EU Circular Economy programs, national bioeconomy funds) that the company could access for circular fertilizer technologies.
Circular.Developing: Co-create small pilot projects on composting, nutrient recovery, or regenerative practices with actors in developing partner countries to access blended finance or development grants.
Circular.Leading: Co-invest in large-scale circular fertilizer infrastructure with support from international financing institutions

Environmental.Awareness: Conduct an internal audit to identify proprietary technologies, processes, or best practices in energy efficiency, nutrient recovery, or pollution prevention that could be valuable for partners in developing countries.
Environmental.Developing: Establish structured knowledge-sharing programs with suppliers or customers abroad. Offer training modules, virtual workshops, or exchange visits focused on environmentally sound fertilizer production methods.
Environmental.Leading: Provide licensing, open-access designs, or reduced-cost technology packages to partners in developing countries for low-carbon fertilizer production.

Economic.Awareness: Encourage SMEs to recognize simple sustainable practices (energy efficiency, waste reduction, optimized raw material use) that lead to cost savings, higher margins, and better cash flow, strengthening tax contributions and reinvestment capacity
Economic.Developing: Report how sustainable operations improve profitability and cash flow, demonstrating increased tax contributions and reinvestment into local operations, reinforcing domestic economic impact.
Economic.Leading: Invest in advanced circular fertilizer technologies (bio-based fertilizers, nutrient recovery, energy-efficient processes) to enhance long-term revenue stability, reduce operational costs, and strengthen contributions to national taxes and reinvestment.

Social.Awareness: Map potential public and private partners (e.g., national agricultural research institutes, technology startups, NGOs) to identify collaboration opportunities in areas like nutrient recovery, green ammonia, or soil health.
Social.Developing: Establish a formal partnership with a local agricultural university to create a training and internship program, building a pipeline of talent skilled in sustainable fertilizer use and production.
Social.Leading: Publicly champion the partnership model by publishing joint case studies and impact reports, and actively advocate for public policies that create a supportive environment for pre-competitive R&D collaborations in the agri-food sector.

Circular.Awareness: Build awareness of the social benefits of reusable/recyclable packaging; collect data on packaging waste and local employment opportunities; identify community partnerships and value-chain gaps using GRI 306-3 and ISO 14001 references.
Circular.Developing: Formalize circular packaging programmes employing local workers in collection, sorting, and reuse; set measurable targets (e.g., tonnes reused, number of local jobs created); integrate monitoring using life-cycle and social indicators.
Circular.Leading: Communicate results (jobs created, packaging reuse rates); collaborate with municipalities, NGOs, and SMEs; replicate community-based circular models regionally.

Environmental.Awareness: Build awareness of heat and climate risks to factory workers; perform vulnerability assessments using ILO and UNDRR frameworks.
Environmental.Developing: Integrate resilience actions into OHS policies: improve ventilation, provide shaded rest areas, hydration, and emergency protocols; set and monitor performance targets.
Environmental.Leading: Publicly disclose climate-resilience measures and outcomes; collaborate with brands, unions, and local authorities to scale good practices.

Economic.Awareness: Map current wage levels and inclusion gaps; benchmark against local living-wage standards; raise awareness of inclusive hiring methods.
Economic.Developing: Establish policies guaranteeing decent wages and inclusive recruitment; set measurable targets (e.g., % above minimum wage, % from disadvantaged backgrounds); implement audits and reporting.
Economic.Leading: Communicate progress in social-impact reporting; engage in sectoral collaborations to scale fair-wage and inclusive-employment models.

Social.Awareness: Identify workers’ access gaps to banking, savings, and benefits; collect baseline data; reference financial inclusion standards.
Social.Developing: Formalize partnerships with financial institutions or NGOs; offer training and savings schemes; define participation and savings-growth targets; monitor impact.
Social.Leading: Communicate outcomes (training reach, improved savings, reduced debt); collaborate with governments and supply-chain partners to replicate inclusion programmes across regions

Circular.Awareness: Assess the origin and type of bio-based inputs used in packaging; distinguish between food-grade feedstocks and secondary biomass such as crop residues, forest by-products, or algae. Promote awareness of life-cycle impacts and competition with food systems using ISO 14040 and ISO 14044 (LCA)
Circular.Developing: Adopt procurement policies prioritizing renewable, non-food and residual biomass feedstocks; integrate traceability of bio-based inputs through ISO 22095 (Chain of Custody) and disclose renewable-material share under GRI 301-1 and 301-2. Collaborate with suppliers to assess feedstock sustainability using FAO’s Sustainability Assessment of Food and Agriculture Systems (SAFA) framework.
Circular.Leading: Invest in R&D for next-generation bio-materials derived from agricultural or forestry residues and industrial side streams. Publicly commit to sourcing only non-food, renewable, and regenerative feedstocks and report progress through transparent life-cycle indicators (ISO 14067, GRI 301).

Environmental.Awareness: Identify all bio-based inputs in packaging and their geographic origin; assess exposure to biodiversity risks such as monoculture feedstocks or land-use change. Raise internal awareness using FAO’s State of the World’s Biodiversity for Food and Agriculture and ISO 14055 guidance on sustainable land management.
Environmental.Developing: Source bio-based raw materials from certified sustainable systems (e.g., FSC, PEFC, organic, or regenerative agriculture). Include biodiversity protection clauses in supplier codes and verify compliance through ISO 19011-based audits. Report sourcing volumes and certification coverage under GRI 304 (Biodiversity).
Environmental.Leading: Collaborate with producers to restore ecosystems and maintain genetic diversity of feedstocks; invest in regenerative agriculture projects that enhance soil health, pollinator habitats, and seed diversity. Publish impact metrics (hectares restored, biodiversity indicators improved) and align targets with the UN Decade on Ecosystem Restoration.

Economic.Awareness: Map current suppliers of bio-based or agricultural feedstocks and identify opportunities to engage small-scale or cooperative producers. Raise awareness of inclusive sourcing models and decent-work principles following ILO Recommendation 204 on the transition from informal to formal economy.
Economic.Developing: Establish inclusive procurement criteria favoring cooperatives and smallholders certified under fair-trade or sustainable agriculture schemes (e.g., Fairtrade International, Rainforest Alliance). Monitor sourcing volumes and price premiums paid; disclose progress in supplier-development indicators under GRI 204-1.
Economic.Leading: Co-create long-term partnerships with small-scale producers through capacity-building, microfinance, and technology transfer. Track income growth and productivity improvements, and report shared-value outcomes aligned with the UN Sustainable Food Systems Roadmap.

Social.Awareness: Assess employee nutritional needs and local food security conditions; promote awareness of healthy, balanced diets and sustainable nutrition using WHO dietary guidelines and FAO’s Sustainable Diets Framework.
Social.Developing: Introduce workplace programs providing nutritious meals, food vouchers, or partnerships with local suppliers of sustainable foods. Integrate nutrition awareness into occupational health and well-being policies and monitor participation rates.
Social.Leading: Implement comprehensive corporate nutrition strategies addressing food access, affordability, and education; measure health outcomes and employee satisfaction; share results in sustainability reports aligned with SDG 2 and GRI 401/403 indicators.

Circular.Awareness: Identify where reused or recycled materials enter the company’s packaging system; raise awareness of potential health and environmental risks associated with contaminants in secondary materials. Map supplier practices using ISO 18602 and ISO 18604 standards, and promote understanding of safe recycling and reuse aligned with the Ellen MacArthur Foundation’s “Vision for a Circular Economy for Plastic Packaging.”
Circular.Developing: Establish procedures to test and certify reused or recycled materials before use in packaging (e.g., migration, heavy metals, and NIAS testing for food-contact applications). Require supplier declarations of conformity and integrate verification steps in procurement and design processes using ISO 18604 and UNEP chemical safety guidance. Disclose data through GRI 301 (Materials) and GRI 306 (Waste).
Circular.Leading: Implement third-party verification of recycled content safety and establish transparent specifications for material reuse in packaging. Collaborate with recyclers and suppliers to develop closed-loop systems ensuring traceability and safety. Communicate testing results and improvement actions in sustainability reports aligned with GRI 301 and ISO 18604.

Environmental.Awareness: Develop a chemical inventory and identify substances of concern across the packaging value chain (e.g., additives, inks, coatings). Align mapping with UNEP’s Global Framework on Chemicals and Ellen MacArthur Foundation’s commitment to eliminate hazardous substances from packaging systems.
Environmental.Developing: Create a restricted substances list aligned with international chemical safety standards; conduct safer alternatives assessments following OECD guidelines. Integrate chemical substitution into ISO 14001 environmental management systems and report progress through GRI 301 (Materials) and 306 (Waste).
Environmental.Leading: Adopt a time-bound strategy to phase out persistent and toxic substances such as PFAS; verify safer alternatives through testing and life-cycle assessments. Partner with suppliers and industry coalitions to “design out” chemical hazards in alignment with circular economy principles.

Economic.Awareness: Raise awareness among management and workers of the benefits of occupational health services and preventive health surveillance. Conduct a baseline assessment of workforce health coverage and workplace safety conditions in line with ILO Convention 161 and Recommendation 171.
Economic.Developing: Allocate funding for periodic medical check-ups and targeted health promotion programs; apply the hierarchy of controls to minimize risks. Track absenteeism, incident rates, and health outcomes through an ISO 45001-aligned management system.
Economic.Leading: Integrate occupational health surveillance with ergonomic, psychosocial, and preventive health programs. Monitor productivity and wellbeing indicators, disclose performance publicly, and benchmark progress against international OHS standards.

Social.Awareness: Build understanding of mental health as an organizational responsibility; identify psychosocial risk factors such as workload, harassment, and poor work-life balance. Promote awareness using WHO and ILO mental health guidance.
Social.Developing: Implement psychosocial risk management under ISO 45003; provide confidential employee assistance programs (EAP) and train managers in supportive leadership. Introduce flexible working arrangements to support well-being and inclusion.
Social.Leading: Integrate mental health support into company-wide OHS and HR policies; set measurable targets (e.g., service uptake, stress reduction, retention rates). Publicly report outcomes under GRI 403 and 401, and share best practices across the industry.

Circular.Awareness: Map roles that influence packaging across the value chain (design, procurement, operations, reverse logistics) and identify skill gaps in circular concepts (reuse models, design for recyclability, reverse flows). Build a training baseline aligned to circular economy principles and basic eco-design.
Circular.Developing: Create role-specific curricula (e.g., designers on design-for-reuse/recyclability; operations on return/refill handling; procurement on circular specifications). Track participation and learning outcomes using GRI 404 disclosures; embed LCA basics for packaging choices.
Circular.Leading: Institutionalize circular training as a competency framework tied to job families and promotion; run hands-on design sprints using EMF methods; certify advanced roles (e.g., internal “circular packaging lead”) and publish outcomes (projects delivered, % portfolio redesigned).

Environmental.Awareness: Adopt an ESD (Education for Sustainable Development) policy for all employees; include core topics in onboarding: resource efficiency, safe and sustainable chemicals, and waste minimization.
Environmental.Developing: Integrate periodic (e.g., annual) training modules with case-based scenarios relevant to operations; include supplier-facing staff. Track completion and skills-upgrading per GRI 404; connect content to EMS and eco-design processes.
Environmental.Leading: Embed ESD across functions (design, procurement, maintenance) with competency assessments and continuous improvement; publish learning KPIs and link to operational metrics (waste reduction, safe-chemical substitution).

Economic.Awareness: Assess current and future skill needs for green and digital transformation (eco-design, LCA, data/automation for material flows). Establish a baseline of training hours and coverage.
Economic.Developing: Fund structured upskilling programs (eco-design via ISO 14006, LCA per ISO 14040/14044; digital skills for take-back/return analytics). Tie learning to process KPIs (line efficiency, defect rates, material yield).
Economic.Leading: Create accredited internal academies and recognized credentials; co-design curricula with unions/partners; publish ROI on training (productivity, waste reductions) under GRI 404-2.

Social.Awareness: Audit participation in training by gender, age, contract type, migration/disability status where lawful; identify barriers (shift patterns, language, accessibility).
Social.Developing: Set targeted inclusion measures (paid time for training, accessible formats, language support, mentoring). Track completion and progression by cohort; disclose under GRI 404 and 405.
Social.Leading: Institutionalize equitable learning pathways (apprenticeships, career ladders) with measurable advancement and pay outcomes; co-create programs with worker reps/ERGs; publish gap-closure targets and progress.

Circular.Awareness: Assess gender balance in teams working on circular-packaging design, R&D, and operations. Build awareness of women’s contribution to circular innovation and sustainable value-chain management using gender-inclusive design principles.
Circular.Developing: Set measurable gender-participation targets for circular-economy projects; ensure women’s representation in decision-making and technical training (eco-design, recycling systems). Monitor gender balance through GRI 405-1 and report progress annually.
Circular.Leading: Establish mentorship and leadership programs for women in circular innovation roles; integrate gender-responsive design into R&D processes; showcase female-led sustainability solutions publicly.

Environmental.Awareness: Assess gender-specific risks and participation levels in environmental programs and safety monitoring; build awareness on differentiated exposure to chemicals, waste, and ergonomics.
Environmental.Developing: Integrate gender considerations into environmental-management systems (ISO 14001 and ISO 45001); ensure women’s representation in sustainability and resource-efficiency committees; provide training on gender-responsive risk assessment.
Environmental.Leading: Adopt a gender-responsive EMS auditing process (ISO 19011); collect sex-disaggregated data on environmental exposures and decisions; communicate outcomes through sustainability reporting and continuous-improvement plans.

Economic.Awareness: Assess employee needs regarding childcare, eldercare, and work-life balance; communicate the social and economic benefits of family-friendly policies aligned with ILO Convention 156 on Workers with Family Responsibilities.
Economic.Developing: Implement paid parental leave, childcare subsidies, and flexible or remote-work options; monitor participation and satisfaction through HR metrics disclosed in GRI 401-2 (benefits) and GRI 405-2 (pay equality).
Economic.Leading: Institutionalize a comprehensive “care-responsibility” framework combining parental leave, eldercare, and flexible arrangements; evaluate outcomes on retention, productivity, and gender balance; publicly disclose policies and results.

Social.Awareness: Adopt a zero-tolerance policy on violence and harassment referencing ILO Convention 190; train managers and employees on recognizing and preventing misconduct; communicate available reporting channels.
Social.Developing: Establish confidential, survivor-centered reporting mechanisms; provide training for grievance officers; monitor case resolution and follow-up actions; disclose system coverage under GRI 406-1 (incidents of discrimination).
Social.Leading: Integrate anti-harassment measures into enterprise risk and OHS systems; conduct independent audits of policy effectiveness; publish aggregated data and continuous-improvement actions in sustainability reports.

Circular.Awareness: Assess water inputs and discharge points across packaging production; identify opportunities for reuse and closed-loop treatment systems. Build awareness of circular-water principles using ISO 46001 and EMF’s industrial water-loop case studies.
Circular.Developing: Install water-reuse technologies (filtration, ultrafiltration, RO, condensate recovery); monitor reuse ratios and water savings. Integrate targets into environmental management under ISO 14001 and disclose progress via GRI 303-3 (water recycled and reused).
Circular.Leading: Achieve closed-loop operation for process water; use treated effluents in non-critical production or utilities; publish verified water-recycling performance and innovation results aligned with ISO 46001 and EMF circular-design benchmarks.

Environmental.Awareness: Map all effluent streams; identify priority pollutants (e.g., inks, coatings, solvents). Build awareness of cleaner-production principles and compliance obligations using UNEP and ISO 14001 frameworks.
Environmental.Developing: Introduce cleaner-production technologies (low-VOC inks, water-based coatings); implement in-plant treatment and monitoring; report pollutant reduction under GRI 303-4 and 303-5. Conduct regular compliance audits per ISO 19011.
Environmental.Leading: Achieve near-zero liquid discharge or equivalent high-reuse performance; publish water-quality indicators (COD, BOD, heavy metals); partner with suppliers to extend cleaner-production standards throughout the value chain.

Economic.Awareness: Quantify water consumption costs across facilities; link water-use data to operational expenses. Communicate the financial benefits of efficiency improvements using UN Water and ISO 46001 guidance.
Economic.Developing: Integrate water-efficiency targets into cost-optimization programs; invest in reuse infrastructure; measure payback periods and cost savings. Disclose results in GRI 303 and economic performance sections (GRI 201).
Economic.Leading: Embed water-efficiency metrics in enterprise resource planning (ERP) and ESG dashboards; monetize water savings in sustainability reporting; reinvest savings into further innovation (e.g., smart sensors, AI monitoring).

Social.Awareness: Assess water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) facilities at all sites; raise awareness of workplace hygiene and its health impacts using WHO/UNICEF WASH guidance.
Social.Developing: Install safe-drinking-water dispensers and gender-segregated sanitation facilities; provide menstrual-hygiene products and awareness training; verify compliance with WHO water-quality standards and national OHS regulations.
Social.Leading: Integrate WASH access into corporate-health and wellbeing programs; audit regularly with third-party verification; disclose coverage and improvement actions in sustainability reports and align with SDG 6.2 indicators.

Circular.Awareness: Map energy flows across production lines to identify waste-heat sources and recovery potential. Build awareness of industrial-symbiosis and energy-loop concepts using ISO 50001 and circular-manufacturing guidance from the Ellen MacArthur Foundation.
Circular.Developing: Install waste-heat recovery (WHR) systems, regenerative burners, or heat-exchanger networks; monitor energy savings and CO₂ reductions. Integrate recovery KPIs within ISO 50001 management reviews and disclose energy-reuse rates in GRI 302-3.
Circular.Leading: Implement fully closed-loop thermal-energy systems or industrial-symbiosis exchanges with nearby facilities; use recovered energy to power ancillary processes. Publicly report avoided-energy consumption and emission savings.

Environmental.Awareness: Quantify total energy mix and emissions baseline; raise awareness of renewable-energy options and certification schemes (e.g., I-REC, Guarantees of Origin). Link transition goals to corporate climate strategy.
Environmental.Developing: Develop a renewable-energy roadmap with clear targets (% of electricity from renewables); implement on-site generation (solar PV, biogas) or long-term PPAs for certified green power. Disclose under GRI 302-1/302-4.
Environmental.Leading: Achieve 100 % renewable electricity or net-zero energy operations verified by third-party certification; collaborate with suppliers to extend renewable adoption across the value chain.

Economic.Awareness: Analyze energy consumption by cost center and identify inefficiencies in machinery, lighting, and compressed-air systems. Communicate potential cost and productivity gains from energy-efficiency investments.
Economic.Developing: Integrate energy-efficiency into capital-planning and maintenance strategies; implement energy audits, high-efficiency motors, and variable-speed drives. Link performance to financial KPIs and disclose ROI and intensity improvements.
Economic.Leading: Institutionalize continual-improvement cycles under ISO 50001; deploy digital-twin or AI systems for predictive optimization; publish verified savings and productivity gains in sustainability and annual reports.

Social.Awareness: Launch basic energy-awareness campaigns covering conservation behaviors, shutdown procedures, and responsible use of lighting, HVAC, and machinery. Include energy literacy in onboarding.
Social.Developing: Provide technical training on energy-management practices and renewable-system operation for maintenance, procurement, and engineering teams; measure participation and learning outcomes.
Social.Leading: Institutionalize ongoing “energy-champion” programs and cross-departmental innovation labs; certify internal experts in ISO 50001; share employee-driven efficiency projects publicly as part of SDG 7 commitments.

Circular.Awareness: Map packaging/product portfolios to identify reuse/refill/take-back opportunities; assess customer segments and reverse-logistics feasibility; align terminology and principles with ISO 59004 and scan EMF case studies for proven models.
Circular.Developing: Pilot circular models (e.g., B2B totes, refill-on-the-go, deposit-return); define operational specs, cleaning standards, and reverse logistics; measure performance with ISO 59020 metrics and disclose material savings under GRI 301/306.
Circular.Leading: Scale commercially viable reuse/take-back with digital tracking, interoperability, and partner ecosystems; integrate circular revenue lines into strategy and publish verified outcomes (return rates, lifetime turns, avoided waste).

Environmental.Awareness: Conduct baseline resource and emissions mapping (energy, materials, water, waste) under ISO 14001; identify hotspots via LCA (ISO 14040/44) and benchmark decoupling potential using UNEP/OECD guidance.
Environmental.Developing: Deploy cleaner-production and resource-efficiency technologies (high-efficiency motors/VSDs, heat recovery, low-carbon materials); integrate targets and M&V via ISO 50001/50015; disclose results in GRI 302 (Energy), 303 (Water), 305 (Emissions), 306 (Waste).
Environmental.Leading: Institutionalize continuous improvement with eco-design (ISO 14006) and supplier engagement; set science-based, time-bound decoupling targets; verify reductions and publish intensity & absolute metrics.

Economic.Awareness: Embed sustainability criteria in the innovation pipeline and portfolio governance; align definitions, roles, and processes with ISO 56002 (innovation management) and screen opportunities using LCA and circular-design principles.
Economic.Developing: Stand up stage-gates with environmental KPIs (recyclability, bio-based share, carbon/water intensity); use digital tools (LCA, digital twins, AI for process optimization); report R&D and capability-building under GRI 201/404.
Economic.Leading: Scale market launches that deliver verified sustainability advantages; co-innovate with suppliers/customers; publish revenue share from “sustainable solutions” and third-party-verified impact metrics.

Social.Awareness: Assess compliance with core labor standards and baseline HR policies (equal pay, non-discrimination, working hours, OSH). Communicate commitments aligned with ILO conventions and GRI disclosures.
Social.Developing: Implement pay-equity analyses and correction plans; ensure secure contracts and predictable schedules; establish worker participation in OSH per ISO 45001 and provide grievance and remediation channels. Disclose metrics (pay gaps, injury rates, turnover).
Social.Leading: Set time-bound targets for equal pay and representation at all levels; adopt living-wage roadmaps; integrate inclusive hiring, apprenticeship, and career-progression pathways; independently assure workforce metrics and publish results.

Circular.Awareness: Identify infrastructure gaps in packaging recovery, sorting, and refill logistics. Map potential synergies with municipalities, industry associations, or recyclers to support circular flows. Align principles with ISO 59004 and Ellen MacArthur Foundation guidance on reuse systems.
Circular.Developing: Co-invest in or co-manage shared collection, cleaning, and refill facilities; establish traceable reverse-logistics partnerships; disclose progress through GRI 301 and 306 indicators.
Circular.Leading: Participate in multi-stakeholder circular infrastructure platforms; develop interoperable refill or deposit-return systems; publicly report system-level material recirculation rates and socio-economic impacts.

Environmental.Awareness: Assess current infrastructure age, efficiency, and emissions intensity; build understanding of Industry 4.0’s role in energy/resource optimization through ISO 50001 and UNIDO’s industrial modernization guidance.
Environmental.Developing: Implement automation, sensor networks, and predictive-maintenance tools to cut energy, water, and material losses; integrate performance data into ISO 14001 environmental-management reviews; disclose progress via GRI 302/305.
Environmental.Leading: Adopt fully digital EMS and real-time environmental-performance dashboards; integrate AI optimization; disclose verified resource-efficiency improvements and emission reductions.

Economic.Awareness: Identify national or regional innovation platforms, clusters, or funding schemes relevant to circular packaging; build awareness of open-innovation benefits using ISO 56002 and UNIDO’s innovation ecosystem resources.
Economic.Developing: Join collaborative R&D or PPP projects; share facilities and data for testing bio-based or recyclable materials; track innovation outputs (patents, prototypes, pilots) and disclose through GRI 203 (Indirect Economic Impacts).
Economic.Leading: Co-lead international innovation consortia; license or scale circular-packaging technologies; publish collaborative R&D outcomes and socio-economic impacts in sustainability reports.

Social.Awareness: Map supplier diversity and SME engagement in the value chain; communicate the economic and social benefits of inclusive industrial participation referencing ILO and UNIDO guidelines.
Social.Developing: Implement inclusive-sourcing programs for SMEs, women-owned, or local enterprises; build capacity through supplier training and fair-contracting policies; disclose supplier-diversity metrics in GRI 204-1.
Social.Leading: Establish long-term partnerships with inclusive suppliers and innovation networks; integrate social-procurement criteria into governance; publish verified socioeconomic impact data and local-employment multipliers.

Circular.Awareness: Map small and underrepresented actors (SMEs, informal recyclers, social enterprises) in your packaging value chain. Build internal awareness of inclusive-procurement benefits and risks of exclusion in circular economies.
Circular.Developing: Adopt inclusive-sourcing criteria favoring SMEs, cooperatives, and underrepresented suppliers; provide training on quality, safety, and traceability; measure local-spending shares under GRI 204-1.
Circular.Leading: Establish long-term partnerships with inclusive suppliers and circular-economy cooperatives; report verified socio-economic impacts (jobs supported, value retained locally).

Environmental.Awareness: Assess employee-engagement structures for inclusiveness (who can make improvement suggestions). Introduce communication channels for all staff to participate in environmental initiatives.
Environmental.Developing: Create formal suggestion and review systems (environmental committees, innovation portals, cross-functional “green teams”); guarantee representation from all employee groups and collect data on participation rates.
Environmental.Leading: Institutionalize inclusive innovation councils combining environmental, DEI, and OHS functions; publish engagement statistics and environmental-improvement outcomes generated by employee input.

Economic.Awareness: Audit pay structures and promotion criteria for transparency; benchmark practices against ILO conventions C100 (Equal Remuneration) and C111 (Discrimination).
Economic.Developing: Publish internal pay-band frameworks and promotion policies; provide employees access to performance-evaluation criteria; conduct gender- and diversity-based pay-gap analysis annually.
Economic.Leading: Institutionalize equal-pay certification or external assurance; link bonuses to sustainability and inclusion KPIs; disclose verified pay-equity results and diversity in leadership.

Social.Awareness: Conduct inclusion-climate surveys; promote cultural-awareness and unconscious-bias training; align internal DEI messaging with the UN Global Compact’s Principle 6 and ILO discrimination conventions.
Social.Developing: Establish formal DEI programs and employee-resource groups (ERGs); provide mentorship and leadership training for underrepresented groups; measure participation and satisfaction rates under GRI 405.
Social.Leading: Embed inclusion goals into corporate KPIs; publish annual diversity metrics and inclusion outcomes; obtain external DEI certification or benchmark via recognized indices.

Circular.Awareness: Map existing municipal or industry-led collection, reuse, and refill initiatives. Identify where company packaging contributes to urban waste streams and raise awareness among staff and partners about extended producer responsibility (EPR).
Circular.Developing: Collaborate with local governments, recyclers, and community enterprises to pilot refill or take-back systems; establish shared data platforms for packaging recovery and reuse tracking.
Circular.Leading: Scale urban reuse and take-back infrastructure through PPPs; co-invest in smart-collection hubs and reverse logistics; publish recovery and reuse metrics under GRI 306.

Environmental.Awareness: Assess site-level environmental impacts—emissions, dust, odour, and noise—using ISO 14001 and local regulatory standards; raise employee and supplier awareness on urban environmental health.
Environmental.Developing: Implement mitigation technologies—low-emission vehicles, particulate filters, acoustic barriers, and waste-heat recovery; monitor progress with GRI 305 and ISO 14031 performance evaluation.
Environmental.Leading: Adopt real-time monitoring for air/noise emissions; transition fleet to electric or alternative fuels; publicly disclose verified performance in sustainability reports and ESG indices.

Economic.Awareness: Identify opportunities for partnerships with micro-enterprises, informal recyclers, and cooperatives bridging urban and rural systems (e.g., bio-based feedstock collection, packaging recovery).
Economic.Developing: Develop inclusive procurement and micro-supply agreements with local cooperatives; provide training, equipment, or logistics support to strengthen their participation in circular material flows.
Economic.Leading: Integrate urban–rural circular partnerships into long-term sourcing and CSR strategy; monitor socioeconomic impact (income growth, waste reduction) and disclose under GRI 203/204.

Social.Awareness: Assess employees’ commuting, housing, and urban-living challenges; raise awareness of links between mobility, wellbeing, and productivity using ILO and WHO frameworks.
Social.Developing: Implement flexible or remote work arrangements, commute-support programs (carpooling, public-transit subsidies, bike storage), and urban-safety audits for all sites.
Social.Leading: Integrate employee urban-wellbeing indicators into sustainability reporting; collaborate with local authorities for safe transport and community infrastructure; disclose progress annually under GRI 401/403.

Circular.Awareness: Set a baseline for packaging formats and end-of-life pathways; align definitions (reuse, recycling, compostability) with recognized standards and circular principles.
Circular.Developing: Adopt time-bound targets for % reusable, recyclable, or compostable packaging; design to ISO packaging standards, and track diversion under GRI.
Circular.Leading: Scale interoperable reuse/take-back systems with verified outcomes; publish packaging circularity and end-of-life performance.

Environmental.Awareness: Inventory all chemical inputs across printing/coating/lamination; identify substances of concern; embed responsibilities within the EMS.
Environmental.Developing: Implement cleaner-production and substitution procedures; set controls for storage/handling, wastewater pre-treatment, and emission prevention; audit and report.
Environmental.Leading: Phase out priority hazardous substances; verify downstream control (e.g., recyclers, contract manufacturers); disclose performance and corrective actions.

Economic.Awareness: Map material sustainability KPIs to cost drivers (energy, water, materials, waste); establish governance for data quality and decision use.
Economic.Developing: Integrate sustainability KPIs into capital budgeting and management reviews; use MFCA and eco-efficiency to link savings and returns; disclose outcomes.
Economic.Leading: Adopt enterprise-wide dashboards tying resource-efficiency and emissions to P&L and investment decisions; link incentives/bonuses to verified sustainability KPIs.

Social.Awareness: Define the priority audiences (operators, sales, customers, end-users); align claims and instructions to recognized guidance and avoid greenwashing.
Social.Developing: Roll out training and customer-facing materials (how to return/reuse/recycle; composting conditions); monitor reach and comprehension; align with packaging end-of-life standards.
Social.Leading: Co-create community or customer partnerships that measurably improve correct disposal/reuse; publish behavior-change outcomes (return rates, contamination reduction).

Circular.Awareness: Map climate-related vulnerabilities in sourcing, manufacturing, logistics, and recycling operations; evaluate exposure to extreme-weather events and resource scarcity.
Circular.Developing: Integrate climate-resilience criteria into supplier selection and circular-design processes; diversify sourcing and build redundancy into reverse-logistics networks.
Circular.Leading: Embed adaptive-capacity KPIs (e.g., supply-chain recovery time, climate-risk scoring) into business continuity; disclose in sustainability and resilience reports.

Environmental.Awareness: Establish a full GHG inventory (Scopes 1–3) using the GHG Protocol; understand baseline emissions and data-collection processes.
Environmental.Developing: Set near- and long-term, science-based GHG-reduction targets; integrate renewable-energy adoption and efficiency upgrades; disclose per GRI 305.
Environmental.Leading: Publicly verify inventories and targets via accredited third-party audits; commit to net-zero under recognized frameworks (SBTi Net-Zero Standard).

Economic.Awareness: Identify transition and physical risks using TCFD categories; assess exposure and potential financial implications.
Economic.Developing: Integrate TCFD-aligned governance, risk, and opportunity assessments into financial statements; conduct scenario analysis and sensitivity testing.
Economic.Leading: Align financial disclosures with IFRS S2 (ISSB 2023) and TCFD; publish climate-adjusted ROI and internal carbon pricing; embed resilience metrics in corporate finance.

Social.Awareness: Develop climate-literacy and awareness campaigns for all staff; explain company climate targets and personal relevance.
Social.Developing: Offer structured internal and supplier-training on energy efficiency, carbon accounting, and adaptation practices; measure learning outcomes and behavioral change.
Social.Leading: Institutionalize annual climate-competence programs; certify “climate champions”; extend learning to customers and community partnerships; disclose participation metrics.

Circular.Awareness: Awarenes: Identify potential pathways for plastic or material leakage into water systems; conduct site-level audits of production, transport, and cleaning operations.
Circular.Developing: Implement containment controls (filter traps, sealed storage, stormwater grates, pellet-handling protocols); track and report spills or material losses annually.
Circular.Leading: Certify operations under pellet-loss prevention standards; engage in local watershed cleanups and circular redesign to eliminate leakage risk across the value chain.

Environmental.Awareness: Awarenes: Map sources of acidifying substances (SO₂, NOₓ, acidic effluents); assess local discharge regulations and downstream water vulnerability.
Environmental.Developing: Install treatment systems (neutralization, scrubbers, effluent pH correction); monitor discharge pH and buffer capacity; disclose data through GRI 303.
Environmental.Leading: Publicly report pH-adjustment performance and downstream impact studies; collaborate with research bodies on ocean chemistry; aim for zero-acidification footprint.

Economic.Awareness: Awarenes: Identify research needs regarding aquatic impacts (microplastics, chemical leachates, biodegradability); map external R&D networks and university or NGO partners.
Economic.Developing: Fund or participate in joint R&D projects evaluating biodegradability, toxicity, and water footprint; report findings in ESG disclosures.
Economic.Leading: Co-develop open-access ocean-health databases or biomaterial R&D platforms; disclose funding for marine-research partnerships and eco-design breakthroughs.

Social.Awareness: Awarenes: Conduct awareness sessions on spill risks, drain mapping, and marine pollution impacts; display clear signage and emergency contacts at operational sites.
Social.Developing: Establish spill-prevention and stormwater-management procedures; conduct periodic drills; introduce incident-reporting systems and track corrective actions.
Social.Leading: Integrate spill-prevention and water-protection training into certification programs; publicly disclose incident data and corrective measures; collaborate with coastal NGOs on water quality.

Circular.Awareness: Awarenwss: Quantify current reliance on virgin vs. recycled/secondary biomass (by mass and spend). Align terminology and targets with circular-economy and chain-of-custody standards; screen feasibility of substituting residues and post-consumer fibers for virgin inputs.
Circular.Developing: Set time-bound targets to increase recycled/secondary content; require chain-of-custody for any remaining virgin inputs; disclose material flows via GRI.
Circular.Leading: Prioritize closed-loop specs with recyclers; publish verified % recycled/secondary content and avoided virgin extraction; integrate circularity metrics into product approvals.

Environmental.Awareness: Awarenwss: Map all bio-based feedstocks to source regions; identify exposure to deforestation, conversion, and soil-degradation risks; align definitions with the Accountability Framework.
Environmental.Developing: Adopt no-deforestation/no-conversion policies; require FSC/PEFC or equivalent certification and ISO 38200/ISO 22095 chain-of-custody; monitor biodiversity impacts and disclose via GRI 304.
Environmental.Leading: Ensure alignment with the Kunming–Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework targets; implement supplier due diligence to meet evolving laws (e.g., EUDR) and publish site-level habitat outcomes.

Economic.Awareness: Awarenwss: Assess nature-related dependencies, impacts, and risks across key commodities; identify potential cost exposures (supply disruption, price volatility, compliance).
Economic.Developing: Integrate TNFD-aligned assessment (LEAP approach) into enterprise risk management; audit suppliers and take actions under GRI 308; set LDN-consistent targets for priority landscapes.
Economic.Leading: Disclose nature-risk governance and metrics (areas at risk, remediation progress, investment in restoration); participate in LDN or landscape-restoration finance mechanisms.

Social.Awareness: Awarenwss: Develop concise biodiversity & land-use training (site risks, material handling, spill/soil protection); link to corporate commitments (no deforestation/conversion, soil conservation).
Social.Developing: Roll out role-specific modules (procurement on due diligence, operations on soil/waste handling); track completion and learning outcomes; include biodiversity KPIs in team objectives.
Social.Leading: Institute annual refreshers and certification for high-impact roles; co-train with suppliers; publicly disclose training coverage and improvements in on-site biodiversity practices.

Circular.Awareness: Map material flows (virgin, recycled, bio-based) and identify disclosure needs for circular attributes (recyclability, reuse readiness, compostability). Align terminology and approach with circular-economy and chain-of-custody standards.
Circular.Developing: Implement chain-of-custody and product-level data capture (e.g., recycled content, recyclability per ISO 18601–18606); disclose material flows and circular metrics in sustainability reports.
Circular.Leading: Publish audited circularity KPIs (e.g., % recycled/secondary content, % recyclable formats) and use recognized measurement frameworks. Offer clients standardized recyclability and end-of-life information.

Environmental.Awareness: Establish an environmental management system with defined aspects/impacts, legal registers, and KPIs; set internal reporting cadences.
Environmental.Developing: Track and disclose core indicators (energy, water, emissions, waste) using GRI topic standards; assure data quality and governance.
Environmental.Leading: Publish externally assured environmental data and targets; provide site-level dashboards where material; align disclosures with recognized frameworks and regulators.

Economic.Awareness: Adopt a formal anti-corruption policy (incl. gifts, hospitality, COI, third-party risk) and communicate zero tolerance; map high-risk processes (procurement, sales).
Economic.Developing: Implement controls and training per ISO 37001 (anti-bribery); embed sustainable and fair procurement practices and supplier due diligence.
Economic.Leading: Conduct independent compliance audits; disclose incidents and remediation; link leadership incentives to ethics and fair-procurement KPIs.

Social.Awareness: Assess current channels for participation (surveys, suggestion systems, safety/environment committees) and who is represented; commit to inclusive engagement.
Social.Developing: Form cross-functional “green & ethics” working groups with elected worker reps; guarantee time and protection for participation; ensure management response and feedback loops.
Social.Leading: Institutionalize participatory governance (co-chaired sustainability councils, joint improvement charters); disclose participation rates, issues raised, and actions taken.

Circular.Awareness: Identify local suppliers and recyclers capable of contributing to closed-loop material cycles; assess logistical and economic barriers to local circularity; map regional associations or industrial symbiosis clusters.
Circular.Developing: Form procurement and logistics partnerships to enhance take-back, material recovery, and reuse; co-develop local infrastructure or hubs for circular packaging collection.
Circular.Leading: Co-invest in regional circular innovation ecosystems; publish joint progress reports on local circularity performance (material recovery rates, job creation, emissions reduction).

Environmental.Awareness: Review available cleaner-production and eco-design technologies; identify partners for potential technology exchange or licensing aligned with best environmental practices.
Environmental.Developing: Engage in bilateral or multi-stakeholder R&D projects on eco-design, recycling, and renewable packaging systems; establish data-sharing agreements and pilot initiatives.
Environmental.Leading: Actively share and scale up proven sustainable technologies regionally; contribute to open innovation platforms; co-publish technical outcomes and life-cycle data.

Economic.Awareness: Identify potential public–private funding programs, EU/UN development finance instruments, or industry consortia supporting circular economy innovation.
Economic.Developing: Collaborate with investors, development agencies, or suppliers to co-fund sustainable packaging R&D or infrastructure; integrate financial metrics into sustainability reporting.
Economic.Leading: Engage in blended-finance consortia or green bonds; publish sustainability-linked investment disclosures; reinvest financial gains into local circular innovation ecosystems.

Social.Awareness: Identify relevant multi-stakeholder networks and associations (e.g., circular economy hubs, chambers of commerce, packaging councils) and map shared objectives.
Social.Developing: Participate actively in peer networks, research alliances, or national circular economy platforms; share lessons and co-develop best-practice guidelines.
Social.Leading: Facilitate regional knowledge-sharing events or open circular data platforms; support local SMEs in capacity-building for sustainable packaging; disclose partnership outcomes.
